# Semaphores

A `Semaphore` controls admission to a limited resource using an initial number
of permits. A thread calling `acquire()` waits until a permit is available or is
interrupted, and `release()` makes a permit available again. When the
application pairs every successful acquisition with exactly one release, this
bounds concurrent access to resources such as database connections. It is like
occupancy control at a public venue: only a fixed number of people may enter at
once, while others wait until someone leaves.

Imagine a service with two database connections receiving five requests at the
same time. This example starts five tasks with a semaphore containing two
permits. A task that reaches `acquire()` when both permits are held waits until
another task releases one. The two-second sleep represents time spent holding a
connection.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this example, attendees can:

- use a semaphore to bound concurrent access to a finite resource;
- explain why a permit is released exactly once after a successful acquisition;
  and
- distinguish a two-permit admission bound from FIFO ordering, fairness, and the
  `release()`-to-`acquire()` visibility guarantee.

## Prerequisite

Install an
[Oracle Java 8](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java8)
JDK or newer and ensure `java` and `javac` resolve to it in the terminal
running this example.

## The program to inspect

This example uses the default, non-fair semaphore. Because each successful
acquisition is paired with exactly one release, its two initial permits ensure
that no more than two tasks use the simulated resource at once. It does not
guarantee which waiting thread acquires the next permit. The task log order
after that point is one possible interleaving, not a FIFO guarantee.

A permit must be released exactly once, and only after `acquire()` has returned
successfully. The inner `finally` ensures that a thread returns its permit even
if the simulated operation fails. If `acquire()` is interrupted, the outer
`catch` does not release anything because no permit was obtained. A semaphore
does not track permit ownership, so an extra `release()` would raise the
available capacity and break the two-connection limit.

```java
    final int numberOfWorkers = 5;
    final int numberOfAllowedPermits = 2;

    /* Allow at most two (numberOfAllowedPermits) tasks to use the simulated
        resource concurrently. */
    final Semaphore semaphore = new Semaphore(numberOfAllowedPermits);

    final List<Thread> threads = new ArrayList<>(numberOfWorkers);
    for (int i = 1; i <= numberOfWorkers; i++) {
        final Runnable task = () -> {
            try {
                log("Task is trying to acquire a permit.");
                semaphore.acquire();
                try {
                    log("Task acquired a permit.");

                    /* Simulate some work with the resource */
                    sleepForTwoSeconds();
                } finally {
                    log("Task releasing the permit.");
                    semaphore.release();
                }
            } catch (final InterruptedException e) {
                Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
                log("Task was interrupted while acquiring the semaphore.");
            }
        };

        final Thread thread = new Thread(task, "Thread-" + i);
        threads.add(thread);
        thread.start();
    }

    log("Wait for all threads to complete");
    waitForAllThreadsToComplete(threads);
```

## Relation to the Java Memory Model (JMM)

A semaphore provides a visibility and ordering guarantee as well as admission
control. The `Semaphore` API specifies that actions before a `release()` happen
before actions after a successful `acquire()` in another thread. Therefore, if a
task updates shared state before returning a permit, a later task that acquires
a permit can observe that update. This is a happens-before relationship; it does
not depend on the semaphore being fair.

This program does not hand shared state from one task to another, so it
demonstrates the two-permit admission bound rather than that visibility
guarantee. Its log and timestamp order are scheduling-dependent and do not prove
a happens-before relationship. Also, with two permits, two tasks may run in the
protected region at once: the semaphore does not make arbitrary
read-modify-write operations atomic or provide mutual exclusion between those
two tasks.

## Guided walkthrough

Run these commands from this example directory. Choose one of the following ways
to run the example.

The example’s one-acquire/one-release protocol establishes the two-permit bound.
The log is one possible execution trace: task acquisition, release, and
timestamp ordering are scheduling dependent and do not establish fairness.

1. Run the example using the
   [Maven `exec` plugin](https://www.mojohaus.org/exec-maven-plugin/).

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean compile exec:exec
   ```
